input.query: why is the sky blue rayleigh scattering

content.text: The Wikipedia result is the most precise about the wavelength relationship, and the atmospheric-optics page covers the sunset case. I will read both properly before citing either — the snippets are the search engine's words, not the sources'. The two fetches are independent, so they go in one turn.
The page states the inverse fourth-power law. Let me check the 450 nm versus 700 nm ratio it claims rather than repeating the number on trust.
The arithmetic confirms the source. I can answer now.

input.answer:
The sky is blue because of Rayleigh scattering: air molecules are far smaller than the wavelength of visible light, and they scatter short wavelengths much more strongly than long ones. [1]

The effect is steep: scattered intensity varies with the inverse fourth power of wavelength. [1] Working that through for 450 nm against 700 nm gives a ratio of about 5.9 — my own arithmetic, which is worth separating from the source, since the page rounds it to 5.5. Either way, sunlight reaching you from every direction other than the sun itself is dominated by blue.

Two details are worth adding. Violet scatters even more strongly than blue, but sunlight contains less of it and the human eye is less sensitive to it, so the sky reads as blue rather than violet. [1] And at sunset the light travels a much longer path through the atmosphere, by which point most of the blue has been scattered away and the reds and oranges are what remain. [2]
